title: Pipelines and Data-Processing Patterns knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Pipelines and Data-Processing Patterns”?
options: Data flow through standard input and output
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Filtering and transforming data” under lesson 77, “Pipelines and Data-Processing Patterns”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Pipelines and Data-Processing Patterns”?
options: Inspect the whole pipeline and use pipefail or PIPESTATUS when upstream failures matter.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the whole pipeline and use pipefail or PIPESTATUS when upstream failures matter.
questions.explanation: Inspect the whole pipeline and use pipefail or PIPESTATUS when upstream failures matter. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Pipelines and Data-Processing Patterns”?
options: Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Check the relevant command statuses immediately and report failures instead of inferring success from output.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
questions.answer_key: Check the relevant command statuses immediately and report failures instead of inferring success from output.
questions.explanation: Check the relevant command statuses immediately and report failures instead of inferring success from output. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
